I'm planning the CrewLink Member Callout assignment using Node.js with Express.js, Next.js with TypeScript, and PostgreSQL.

Before designing the system, I want to establish my own understanding of the requirements.

My initial interpretation is:

Each union local is an isolated tenant Members and leadership must not access another local's data
Members and leadership have different permissions.
Push delivery can fail, and members may be offline for hours or days.
Retries and worker restarts must not cause duplicate callouts or duplicate recipient records.
AI-generated callouts must remain drafts until a human leader approves them.
Delivery status must be tracked per recipient, not just per announcement.

Create only a concise draft of the Requirements section for DESIGN.md. Separate confirmed requirements from assumptions and open questions. Point out any incorrect assumptions or important requirements I've missed.

Do not write code, create other files, or design the complete architecture yet. I want to review and understand the requirements before moving forward.


Actual breif:
#attachment:Pasted text #1

**This exercise covers the whole job, not just the backend. You'll take a messy, non-technical ask from a fictional stakeholder and turn it into a scoped plan 

yourself, then design the system, then build a thin slice across the front end, the back end, and how it runs behind a load balancer. Part 0 and Part A carry the most weight, so don't let Part B's build time crowd out your design time. Nobody sent you a clean spec; that's deliberate. AI tools are expected and encouraged throughout; see Section 5 for what to share. 

01 The Ask 

CrewLink is a fictional platform for labour unions, invented for this exercise. Union members are working people: electricians, transit operators, sheet-metal workers. Union leadership uses the platform to reach them. 

Below is the kind of message a business manager might realistically send. It's 

invented, but written the way these things actually get written: vague, a little 

urgent, not organized for an engineer's benefit. 

SLACK MESSAGE · DENISE OKAFOR, BUSINESS MANAGER, LOCAL 27 (FICTIONAL) 

"Hey, we keep missing people on the callouts. Half of Local 27 didn't know about Thursday's emergency meeting until it was too late and it's caused real problems with the contractor situation. Members are saying they never got anything, or they got it but by the time they saw it the meeting was already over. Also I need to know before I leave the hall on the day of a callout who's actually coming so I'm not standing in an empty room. Oh and can members outside our local see the wireman apprentices' contact info too? someone mentioned that during onboarding and I want to make sure that's not happening. We need this sorted before the next round of contract talks, whenever that ends up being scheduled." 

That's it. That's the brief. 

The numbers you're designing for 

Union locals on one platform 43

Members total 187,000 

Largest local (one callout goes to all of them) 22,400 

Push notifications that silently fail roughly 5–10% How long a member can be offline hours, sometimes days 

Members work in basements, elevator shafts, underground transit and rural 

highway. Their phone being off the network for a day is normal, not an edge case. 

TWO RULES THAT SHAPE EVERYTHING 

Rule 1: nobody sees or touches data outside their own access. One local's information must never reach another local's members or leadership, and a member must never be able to act with a leader's permissions. Union membership is sensitive; if it leaks, or if someone acts beyond their role, members can lose their jobs. 

Rule 2: a retry or a restart must not deliver twice to the same member. Leadership will retry a send that looks stuck, and a crashed process will restart mid-send. 22,400 people must not get it twice either way. 

Part 0: turn that into requirements 

Before any design or code: write a short Requirements section at the top of 

DESIGN.md . Four things, no more than a few sentences each: 

Restate what you're actually going to build, in your own words, as if 

explaining it back to Denise. 

List your assumptions for everything the message doesn't specify: who 

exactly this is for, what "immediately" means, whether confirming attendance is 

required or optional, what counts as done. 

Flag anything in the message that concerns you. There is at least one thing 

in there worth flagging before you build anything. 

Write the questions you'd ask Denise if you could. Up to three. Nobody will 

answer them (this isn't a live channel) but write them anyway, and say what you assumed instead since you couldn't ask. 

02 Part A: the design 

Below your Part 0 requirements, in the same DESIGN.md . Answer these four 

directly. Your answers are the record of the decisions you made and the 

alternatives you rejected, so a reviewer isn't guessing why the system looks the way it does. Max 1,500 words for these four prompts (Part 0's requirements 

section is separate, keep that short too) plus one diagram.

1. Data model 

The tables and their important fields. How do you record who a message went to and what each of them did with it: nothing, read it, acknowledged it, said they're coming, said they can't? 

2. The send path 

Leadership presses Send at 14:02. Walk us through what happens, in order, until 22,400 phones have buzzed. What happens inside that first request, and what happens somewhere else? How long does leadership wait before the UI responds? And once it's sending: if four people in the office have the status screen open, watching sent/read/acknowledged counts update, what stops that from hammering the database every second? 

3. The two rules, by design 

Where does Rule 1 get enforced? Both the boundary between locals and the boundary between a member and leadership, and what happens when someone adds a new endpoint next year and forgets about it? What makes Rule 2 true when the request is retried, or when the process handling it restarts partway through? Not "we disable the button", but what in the system makes the same member unreachable twice? And separately: how would you find out in production if either of these had already broken? 

4. A diagram 

Boxes and arrows showing the pieces and what talks to what, include the load balancer and your instances. Excalidraw, draw.io, Mermaid, or a photo of a whiteboard, all equally fine. We are not judging how it looks. 

03 Part B: build a slice 

Now show one part of that design actually running. Not the whole thing: the spine, front end included. 

Backend, required 

Create and send an announcement to an audience (one local, optionally 

narrowed by work classification), producing whatever per-recipient records your 

design calls for 

A member can read it and acknowledge it, via an endpoint is fine. RSVP 

("coming" / "can't") is Part A design only, not required in the build. 

Rules 1 and 2 genuinely enforced, the way your design says 

One AI feature, see below 

Front end, required, keep it small, your choice of Next.js or Flutter 

One screen for leadership: write a title and body (or paste the messy note and use the AI feature), pick a local, hit send, and see the counts update: sent, read, 

acknowledged. That's the whole screen. Build it as a Next.js page or as a Flutter 

screen, whichever you're strongest in. Same slice, same scoring, either way.

SCOPE RELIEF, PLEASE READ 

Unstyled is a completely acceptable submission. An unstyled Next.js page 

with a form and a table, or an unstyled Flutter widget tree, either is fine. We are 

not scoring how it looks, only that leadership could actually use it. 

A member-facing screen is optional. An endpoint the member calls to read 

and acknowledge is enough, no UI required on that side. 

Real push notifications are not required. Log them, or write them to a table. 

Nobody needs FCM credentials for this. 

Running locally is fine. docker compose up , or README steps we can follow 

in ten minutes. Deploying is optional, don't spend hours on hosting. 

DEVOPS BONUS, OPTIONAL, DO THIS ONLY IF THE REST IS SOLID 

Add (or extend) a docker-compose.yml to run two instances of your backend behind a load balancer: nginx or HAProxy, round-robin, minimal config is fine. Then send an announcement, hitting either instance at random for every request, and show that Rule 2 still holds: no double send, even across instances. 

This is worth more than it sounds: a "have we already sent this" check kept in one process's memory quietly stops working the moment there's a second process. We'll ask about this in the interview whether or not you build it, so thinking it through counts even if you skip the compose file. 

The AI feature 

Leadership types the way busy people type: 

REAL EXAMPLE INPUT 

"emergency mtg thurs 6pm hall re: contractor pulling crews off the westside job, EVERYONE needs to be there this is the third time" 

Turn it into a clear title and body, plus a push preview of 120 characters or 

fewer. Show it as a draft that must be approved before it can send. Any model provider. 

What we're looking at is the integration, not the prompt: what happens when the provider is slow or down, and whether generated text can reach 22,400 members without a human agreeing to it. 

Stack & seed data 

Backend: Django + DRF + Postgres preferred. That's what we run and read 

fastest. Solid work in another stack still counts. 

Seed 2 locals yourself with a re-runnable script: ~2,000 members in one, 200 in the other, across 3–4 classifications, plus one leadership and one member login per local. Enough to catch a careless query, small enough to skip the scale

problem from Part A. Also seed one already-sent announcement in the larger local, with its recipient rows; the README's Test Accounts section needs its id. 

ONE MORE THING YOUR README NEEDS: ## TEST ACCOUNTS 

Add a section with this exact heading, containing a fenced JSON block with: both logins for each local, the id of one existing announcement belonging to the larger local, the id of a member in the other local, and the method/path/auth style for the handful of endpoints you built. Five minutes of work, and it's what lets us run requests against your submission without emailing you for database ids. Once you submit, we'll spin up your docker compose (or follow your README) and run requests against your running API ourselves as part of the review: the same kind of requests a real client would make, using the Test Accounts section above, nothing beyond what this brief already describes. 

04 Starting point 

Three tables to start from. How you model recipients and their status, and how you distinguish a leadership account from a member account for Rule 1, is deliberately missing. Those are the decisions we're actually interested in. 

Change any of this if your design says otherwise; just tell us why. 

locals 

 id uuid 

 name text -- "Local 27" 

members 

 id uuid 

 local_id uuid -> locals 

 full_name text 

 email text 

 classification text -- "Journeyman Wireman", "Apprentice 3rd Year"  status text -- active | retired | suspended 

announcements 

 id uuid 

 local_id uuid -> locals 

 title text 

 body text 

 needs_ack boolean 

 sent_at timestamptz -- null until sent 

 created_at timestamptz

response.value:
Your proposal has the right core entities. The key refinement is to make **local-scoped relationships explicit**: a global user role or a single `local_id` on `users` is too restrictive if someone can hold different roles or memberships in different locals.

### Entities and relationships

- **`locals`** — one row per tenant, keyed by UUID.
- **`users`** — authentication identity and credentials, independent of any local. Keep local membership and leadership roles out of a global `role` field.
- **Local access records** — represent member and leader access as local-scoped relationships, such as `local_members` and `local_leaders`. A person can be a member, a leader, or both; each relationship is tied to a specific local.
- **`classifications`** — optionally normalize work classifications into local-scoped rows. This prevents inconsistent spellings and makes audience filtering reliable.
- **`members`** (or member profile fields on `local_members`) — local-scoped profile information: classification, active/retired/suspended status, and any local-specific contact details. If contact information is sensitive, avoid placing it on a globally shared user record.
- **`announcements`** — belongs to one local and records its author, title, body, push preview, acknowledgement requirement, and draft/approval/send timestamps or state. The author and approver must have leadership access to that same local. Keep AI output in draft form until an eligible leader approves it.
- **`announcement_recipients`** — one row per announcement and member, representing the audience snapshot at send time. Track push-provider outcome separately from member actions: queued/attempted/provider-accepted (and provider delivery receipt if available), read, acknowledged, and optional RSVP (“coming” / “can’t”). A missing RSVP should remain distinct from “can’t.”
- **`delivery_attempts`** — append-only attempt history for retries, including timestamps and provider outcomes. This prevents the recipient’s current status from erasing retry history. An outbox/job record may also be needed to durably schedule work, but its processing details belong in the send-path design.

### Constraints and indexes

Use UUID primary keys and add composite uniqueness such as `UNIQUE (local_id, id)` on local-owned records so other tables can reference them as `(local_id, record_id)`. Then give recipients **both** a composite foreign key to `(local_id, announcement_id)` and one to `(local_id, member_id)`. This makes a recipient row that combines a member from one local with an announcement from another invalid at the database level.

Add `UNIQUE (announcement_id, member_id)` to `announcement_recipients` to prevent duplicate recipient rows on retries. Use foreign keys from announcement author/approver to the corresponding local-leader relationship. For members, constrain status to the allowed values; for classifications, use a local-scoped foreign key so a member cannot reference another local’s classification. Add checks for valid state combinations where practical—for example, an approved announcement must have an approver and approval time.

Useful indexes include:
- Members by `(local_id, status, classification_id)` for audience selection.
- Announcements by `(local_id, created_at)` and, if commonly filtered, `(local_id, status, created_at)`.
- Recipients by `(announcement_id, member_id)` for uniqueness, and `(local_id, announcement_id, delivery_status)` for local-scoped status counts.
- Delivery attempts by `(recipient_id, attempted_at)`.

Primary-key and unique constraints create indexes automatically; PostgreSQL does **not** automatically index the referencing side of every foreign key, so add indexes based on the lookups and joins above.

### Important limitations

A unique recipient row prevents duplicate **database records**, but does not by itself guarantee that an external push provider never sends twice. Provider acceptance and actual receipt are also different facts; use precise status names rather than treating “sent” as “received.”

Finally, composite foreign keys prevent cross-local references, not cross-local reads. They are an important database safeguard, but by themselves they do not enforce who may query the data. A globally scoped `users.role` is also insufficient: authorization must be based on the user’s role in the specific local.

 # Part A: The design
 
 ## 1. Data model
 
 - **`locals`** stores each union local. **`users`** stores authentication identity only; it has no global member/leader role. **`local_members`** stores a user's local-specific member profile, including name, contact details, classification, and active/retired/suspended status. **`local_leaders`** grants leadership access for a specific local.  - **`classifications`** stores work classifications scoped to a local, with a unique `(local_id, id)` key. `local_members` references it using `(local_id, classification_id)`, preventing a profile from using another local's classification.
 - **`announcements`** belongs to a local and stores its author, title, body, push preview, acknowledgement requirement, draft/approval/send state, and relevant timestamps. Its author is constrained by a composite foreign key `(local_id, author_user_id)` to `local_leaders`; approval, when recorded, is likewise tied to a leader in that local. Give announcements a unique `(local_id, id)` key for downstream composite references.
 - **`announcement_recipients`** has one row per audience member, with `(announcement_id, member_id)` unique. Store `local_id` on the row and use composite foreign keys `(local_id, announcement_id)` and `(local_id, member_id)` to the corresponding announcement and `local_members` keys. Materialize these rows from the eligible audience at send time: they are the audience snapshot, not a live query whose membership changes later. Keep push-provider state (for example queued, attempted, accepted, failed, or provider-confirmed if supported) separate from `read_at`, `acknowledged_at`, and nullable RSVP (`coming` / `can't`); no RSVP is distinct from “can't.”

 Use PostgreSQL `CHECK` constraints or enums for finite status/action values and checks for valid approval state/timestamp combinations. Index audience selection on `local_members (local_id, status, classification_id)`, announcement listings on `(local_id, created_at)`, recipient counts/lookups on `(local_id, announcement_id, push_status)` and `(announcement_id, read_at)` / `(announcement_id, acknowledged_at)`, and attempt history on `(recipient_id, attempted_at)`. Primary keys and unique constraints provide indexes for their keys; add indexes on foreign-key columns used for joins and lookups.
 
 These constraints reject invalid cross-local references and duplicate recipient records; they do not replace endpoint authorization checks. Likewise, a unique recipient row does not guarantee exactly-once delivery by an external push provider.

response.value:
## Part A, Question 2: The send path

1. **Accept and commit the send.** An authorized Express endpoint verifies that the leader can send for the announcement’s local and that the announcement is approved. In one PostgreSQL transaction, it marks the announcement as sending, snapshots the eligible members into `announcement_recipients`, and records durable notification work in an outbox. Unique constraints on recipients—and an idempotency key for the send request—make a repeated request reuse the same send rather than create another audience. The endpoint responds after commit with an accepted/in-progress status; it does not wait for 22,400 pushes.

2. **Process work asynchronously.** Workers poll the PostgreSQL outbox, claim jobs in small batches using row locks such as `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and record a lease or claim state. They send notifications outside the database transaction, then persist provider outcomes and attempt history. Short transactions avoid holding database locks while waiting on the provider. Transient errors can be retried with backoff; permanent failures should be recorded rather than retried indefinitely.

3. **Recover safely after restarts.** A worker’s lease expires if it crashes, allowing another worker to reclaim unfinished work. The recipient’s unique row prevents duplicate recipient records, and durable job state prevents a process restart from losing queued work. However, there is an unavoidable ambiguity if a worker crashes after the provider accepts a push but before PostgreSQL records that result. ## Part A, Question 3: The two rules, by design

**Rule 1 — access isolation and roles.** Express authenticates each request and derives the user identity from a verified credential—not from a client-supplied `local_id` or role. Authorization is default-deny and checks the user’s role for the resource’s local on every endpoint. Queries are scoped to that local; composite foreign keys prevent cross-local relationships in stored records. PostgreSQL row-level security can provide defense in depth, provided the application sets the local context transactionally and the application role cannot bypass RLS. Workers use a separate, least-privilege service identity and process only the local and recipient recorded on each job. Record successful and denied access-sensitive actions in an audit log with actor, local, action, resource, and timestamp; do not log credentials or unnecessary member data.

**Rule 2 — retries and restarts.** PostgreSQL is the source of truth for send state. A transaction creates the recipient snapshot and one durable outbox job per recipient; uniqueness constraints prevent duplicate recipient and job records. Workers claim jobs atomically with locks and leases, and update outcomes so retries or expired leases can resume unfinished work. The send-request idempotency key ensures a retried API request refers to the same send. Use provider idempotency keys when supported; without them, a crash after provider acceptance but before recording success can cause a duplicate push, so exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed. Keep that uncertainty visible in per-recipient delivery status and attempt history.

**Safeguards and verification.** Test that members and leaders from another local cannot read, change, send, or infer protected records by altering IDs; test database constraints reject cross-local references. Run duplicate and concurrent send-request tests, and worker retry/restart tests across multiple worker instances, checking that each recipient has one record and that provider idempotency is used where available. Audit and monitor denied cross-local access, authorization failures, stuck/expired jobs, repeated provider attempts, and discrepancies between claimed outcomes and provider responses.

Leaders need timely visibility into who has read, acknowledged, or plans to attend. - AI-generated title, body, and push preview (120 characters or fewer) must remain a draft until a human leader approves sending. ## Assumptions - Unless confirmed otherwise, the send audience is active members of the selected local, optionally filtered by classification; retired and suspended members are excluded. - No response is required by default. Acknowledgment and an attendance RSVP ("coming" / "can't") are distinct actions; RSVP is needed for the design, but not the required build slice. - Members can retrieve a sent callout after reconnecting; push is a prompt, not the only way to access it. What does "immediately" mean, and which notification states should leadership see as sent or delivered when a push fails or a member is offline? Assumed send begins promptly, with recipient-level progress and later access. 3. Should attendance responses be optional or required, by what deadline, and may members change them? Assumed optional unless a callout explicitly requests an RSVP. # Part A: The design ## 1. Data model - **`locals`** stores each union local. **`users`** stores authentication identity only; it has no global member/leader role. **`local_members`** stores a user's local-specific member profile, including name, contact details, classification, and active/retired/suspended status. **`local_leaders`** grants leadership access for a specific local. Both local-access tables use `(local_id, user_id)` as a primary or unique key, with foreign keys to `locals` and `users`. Primary keys and unique constraints provide indexes for their keys; add indexes on other foreign-key columns used for joins and lookups. These constraints reject invalid cross-local references and duplicate recipient records; they do not replace endpoint authorization checks. Likewise, a unique recipient row does not guarantee exactly-once delivery by an external push provider. ## 2.  ## Open questions for Denise
 1. Who is eligible for a callout: active members only, and how should classification changes or membership changes after sending affect it? Assumed active members at send time.
 2. What does "immediately" mean, and which notification states should leadership see as sent or delivered when a push fails or a member is offline? Assumed send begins promptly, with recipient-level progress and later access.
 3. Should attendance responses be optional or required, by what deadline, and may members change them? Assumed optional unless a callout explicitly requests an RSVP.
 
 # Part A: The design
 
 ## 1. Data model
 
 - **`locals`** stores each union local. **`users`** stores authentication identity only; it has no global member/leader role. **`local_members`** stores a user's local-specific member profile, including name, contact details, classification, and active/retired/suspended status. **`local_leaders`** grants leadership access for a specific local. Both local-access tables use `(local_id, user_id)` as a primary or unique key, with foreign keys to `locals` and `users`. A user can have different or multiple local relationships without those permissions becoming global.
 - **`classifications`** stores work classifications scoped to a local, with a unique `(local_id, id)` key. `local_members` references it using `(local_id, classification_id)`, preventing a profile from using another local's classification.
 - **`local_members`** has its own UUID `id`, a foreign key `user_id` to `users`, and unique `(local_id, user_id)` and `(local_id, id)` keys. Thus recipient `member_id` always means `local_members.id`, never the authentication `users.id`.
 - **`announcements`** belongs to a local and stores its author, title, body, push preview, acknowledgement requirement, draft/approval/send state, and relevant timestamps. Its author is constrained by a composite foreign key `(local_id, author_user_id)` to `local_leaders`; approval, when recorded, is likewise tied to a leader in that local. Give announcements a unique `(local_id, id)` key for downstream composite references.
 - **`announcement_recipients`** has UUID `id`, `local_id`, `announcement_id`, and `member_id`, with `(announcement_id, member_id)` unique and `(local_id, id)` unique. Composite foreign keys `(local_id, announcement_id)` and `(local_id, member_id)` reference the corresponding announcement and `local_members` keys. Materialize these rows from the eligible audience at send time: they are the audience snapshot, not a live query whose membership changes later. Keep push-provider state separate from `read_at`, `acknowledged_at`, and nullable RSVP (`coming` / `can't`); no RSVP is distinct from “can't.”
 - **`outbox_jobs`** has UUID `id`, `local_id`, `recipient_id` (the recipient row's `announcement_recipients.id`), status, attempt count, `available_at`, and lease fields such as `lease_until`. A unique `(local_id, recipient_id)` permits one durable job per recipient; a composite foreign key `(local_id, recipient_id)` references `announcement_recipients (local_id, id)`. Workers therefore process the stored local and recipient row, not a client-supplied audience.
 - **`send_requests`** records the send idempotency key, local, leader user, announcement, and request hash. A unique `(local_id, leader_user_id, idempotency_key)` scopes key reuse; matching retries return the recorded send, while a different request hash is rejected. Its leader reference is constrained to `(local_id, leader_user_id)` in `local_leaders`.
 - **`delivery_attempts`** records each push attempt against its recipient, including attempt time and provider outcome, so retries do not erase history. Use a foreign key to `announcement_recipients`; use a stable provider idempotency key per recipient if the provider supports one.
 
 Use PostgreSQL `CHECK` constraints or enums for finite status/action values and checks for valid approval state/timestamp combinations. Index audience selection on `local_members (local_id, status, classification_id)`, announcement listings on `(local_id, created_at)`, recipient counts/lookups on `(local_id, announcement_id, push_status)` and `(announcement_id, read_at)` / `(announcement_id, acknowledged_at)`, outbox claiming on `(status, available_at)` and lease recovery on `(status, lease_until)`, and attempt history on `(recipient_id, attempted_at)`. Primary keys and unique constraints provide indexes for their keys; add indexes on other foreign-key columns used for joins and lookups.
 
 These constraints reject invalid cross-local references and duplicate recipient records; they do not replace endpoint authorization checks. Likewise, a unique recipient row does not guarantee exactly-once delivery by an external push provider.
 
 ## 2. The send path
 
 The authenticated Express endpoint verifies the leader's local permission and that the announcement is approved. The client supplies an idempotency key for the send operation. In one PostgreSQL transaction, the endpoint records the key and request hash in `send_requests`, snapshots eligible members into `announcement_recipients`, creates **one `outbox_jobs` row per recipient**, and marks the announcement as sending. A unique constraint on the scoped key makes a matching repeated request return the original send result rather than create a new audience; reusing the key with a different request hash is rejected. Recipient and outbox uniqueness also prevent duplicate rows/jobs.
 
 After commit, the endpoint returns an accepted/in-progress response; it does not wait for all pushes. Workers claim small batches of ready outbox rows in short transactions using row locks such as `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, recording a lease and attempt count. Each job supplies its stored `local_id` and `recipient_id`; workers load and verify that recipient and its member profile in that local, then call the provider outside the transaction and persist the outcome. Transient errors are rescheduled with backoff; permanent errors or exhausted retries are marked failed for review. If a worker crashes, its lease expires and another worker can reclaim the job. A stable provider idempotency key per recipient and announcement prevents repeated provider sends when supported. Without provider support, a crash after provider acceptance but before recording success leaves an ambiguous result: retrying can duplicate a push, while not retrying can lose it. Exactly-once external push delivery cannot be guaranteed in that case.
 
 Push is only a prompt. Members fetch their persisted callouts through the authenticated API and can sync after reconnecting, so being offline or missing a push does not remove access. Provider outcomes remain separate from read, acknowledgment, and RSVP actions.
 
 ## 3. The two rules, by design
 
 **Rule 1—local isolation and roles:** Express authenticates requests and derives the user identity from a verified credential, never a client-supplied role. Default-deny authorization checks the user's membership or leadership relationship for the specific local and action on every endpoint; queries are scoped to that local. Composite foreign keys reject cross-local references. PostgreSQL row-level security can add defense in depth if the app role cannot bypass it and each transaction sets its local context safely. Workers use a separate least-privilege identity and validate job local/recipient references. Append audit records for sensitive reads and mutations, including actor, local, action, resource, outcome, and timestamp; exclude credentials and unnecessary personal data.
 
 **Rule 2—duplicate processing:** The transactional send snapshot, unique recipient/job constraints, persisted idempotency key, and leased outbox claims make request retries and worker restarts safe at the database/job level. Provider idempotency is needed to prevent duplicate external pushes across the acceptance/recording crash window; without provider support, exactly-once push delivery cannot be guaranteed.
 
 Test cross-local access by attempting reads and mutations with another local's IDs and by inserting mismatched-local rows directly; verify denial

 - "No duplicates" applies to both creating duplicate recipient records and sending duplicate notifications on retries. Whether this can be guaranteed at the push-provider boundary depends on provider behavior and needs to be defined.
 
 ## Concerns and gaps
 - The question about members outside a local seeing apprentices' contact information may indicate an existing exposure, not just a future requirement. Treat this as a potential incident to investigate and contain before relying on a new feature's access controls.
 - A unique recipient record alone does not establish that a member was notified, received the callout, read it, acknowledged it, or RSVP'd. Those states must not be conflated, especially when push can fail silently.
 - "Immediately" and "before I leave the hall" have no measurable timing target; no RSVP deadline, edit policy, or rule for late audience changes is given.

 1. Who is eligible for a callout: active members only, and how should classification changes or membership changes after sending affect it? Assumed active members at send time.

 ## Open questions for Denise
 1. Who is eligible for a callout: active members only, and how should classification changes or membership changes after sending affect it? Assumed active members at send time.
 2. What does "immediately" mean, and which notification states should leadership see as sent or delivered when a push fails or a member is offline? Assumed send begins promptly, with recipient-level progress and later access.
 3. Should attendance responses be optional or required, by what deadline, and may members change them? Assumed optional unless a callout explicitly requests an RSVP.
 
 # Part A: The design
 
 ## 1. Data model
 
 - **`locals`** stores each union local. **`users`** stores authentication identity only; it has no global member/leader role. **`local_members`** stores a user's local-specific member profile, including name, contact details, `classification_id`, and active/retired/suspended status. **`local_leaders`** grants leadership access for a specific local. Both local-access tables use `(local_id, user_id)` as a primary or unique key, with foreign keys to `locals` and `users`. A user can have different or multiple local relationships without those permissions becoming global.
 - **`classifications`** stores work classifications scoped to a local, with a unique `(local_id, id)` key. `local_members` references it using `(local_id, classification_id)`, preventing a profile from using another local's classification.
 - **`local_members`** has its own UUID `id`, a foreign key `user_id` to `users`, and unique `(local_id, user_id)` and `(local_id, id)` keys. Thus recipient `member_id` always means `local_members.id`, never the authentication `users.id`.
 - **`announcements`** belongs to a local and stores its author, title, body, push preview, acknowledgement requirement, draft/approval/send state, and relevant timestamps. Its author is constrained by a composite foreign key `(local_id, author_user_id)` to `local_leaders`; approval, when recorded, is likewise tied to a leader in that local. Give announcements a unique `(local_id, id)` key for downstream composite references.
 - **`announcement_recipients`** has UUID `id`, `local_id`, `announcement_id`, and `member_id`, with `(announcement_id, member_id)` unique and `(local_id, id)` unique. Composite foreign keys `(local_id, announcement_id)` and `(local_id, member_id)` reference the corresponding announcement and `local_members` keys. Materialize these rows from the eligible audience at send time: they are the audience snapshot, not a live query whose membership changes later. Keep push-provider state separate from `read_at`, `acknowledged_at`, and nullable RSVP (`coming` / `can't`); no RSVP is distinct from “can't.”
 - **`outbox_jobs`** has UUID `id`, `local_id`, `recipient_id` (the recipient row's `announcement_recipients.id`), status, attempt count, `available_at`, and lease fields such as `lease_until`. A unique `(local_id, recipient_id)` permits one durable job per recipient; a composite foreign key `(local_id, recipient_id)` references `announcement_recipients (local_id, id)`. Workers therefore process the stored local and recipient row, not a client-supplied audience.
 - **`send_requests`** records the send idempotency key, local, leader user, announcement, and request hash. A unique `(local_id, leader_user_id, idempotency_key)` scopes key reuse; matching retries return the recorded send, while a different request hash is rejected. Its leader reference is constrained to `(local_id, leader_user_id)` in `local_leaders`.
 - **`delivery_attempts`** records each push attempt against its recipient, including attempt time and provider outcome, so retries do not erase history. Use a foreign key to `announcement_recipients`; use a stable provider idempotency key per recipient if the provider supports one.
 
 Use PostgreSQL `CHECK` constraints or enums for finite status/action values and checks for valid approval state/timestamp combinations. Index audience selection on `local_members (local_id, status, classification_id)`, announcement listings on `(local_id, created_at)`, recipient counts/lookups on `(local_id, announcement_id, push_status)` and `(announcement_id, read_at)` / `(announcement_id, acknowledged_at)`, outbox claiming on `(status, available_at)` and lease recovery on `(status, lease_until)`, and attempt history on `(recipient_id, attempted_at)`. Primary keys and unique constraints provide indexes for their keys; add indexes on other foreign-key columns used for joins and lookups.
 
 These constraints reject invalid cross-local references and duplicate recipient records; they do not replace endpoint authorization checks. Likewise, a unique recipient row does not guarantee exactly-once delivery by an external push provider.
 
 ## 2. The send path
 
 The authenticated Express endpoint verifies the leader's local permission and that the announcement is approved. The client supplies an idempotency key for the send operation. In one PostgreSQL transaction, the endpoint records the key and request hash in `send_requests`, snapshots eligible members into `announcement_recipients`, creates **one `outbox_jobs` row per recipient**, and marks the announcement as sending. A unique constraint on the scoped key makes a matching repeated request return the original send result rather than create a new audience; reusing the key with a different request hash is rejected. Recipient and outbox uniqueness also prevent duplicate rows/jobs.
 
 After commit, the endpoint returns an accepted/in-progress response; it does not wait for all pushes. Workers claim small batches of ready outbox rows in short transactions using row locks such as `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, recording a lease and attempt count. Each job supplies its stored `local_id` and `recipient_id`; workers load and verify that recipient and its member profile in that local, then call the provider outside the transaction and persist the outcome. Transient errors are rescheduled with backoff; permanent errors or exhausted retries are marked failed for review. If a worker crashes, its lease expires and another worker can reclaim the job. A stable provider idempotency key per recipient and announcement prevents repeated provider sends when supported. Without provider support, a crash after provider acceptance but before recording success leaves an ambiguous result: retrying can duplicate a push, while not retrying can lose it. Exactly-once external push delivery cannot be guaranteed in that case.
 
 Push is only a prompt. Members fetch their persisted callouts through the authenticated API and can sync after reconnecting, so being offline or missing a push does not remove access. Provider outcomes remain separate from read, acknowledgment, and RSVP actions.

 # CrewLink
 
 ## Backend setup
 
 The backend uses Express, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL 13 or later is required for `gen_random_uuid()`.
 
 1. Create a PostgreSQL database and user (or use an existing local development database).
 2. From the `backend` directory, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `DATABASE_URL` to the connection string for that database. `PORT` defaults to `4000`.
    Set `JWT_SECRET` to a unique cryptographically random secret of at least 32 bytes; the API will not start without it. Do not reuse the example value or commit the secret.
 3. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
 4. Apply the initial schema with `npm run db:migrate`.
 5. Start the development server with `npm run dev`. Check `http://localhost:4000/health` for database connectivity.
 6. Run `npm run build` to type-check and compile; run `npm start` to start the compiled server.
 
 The migration is tracked in `schema_migrations` and can safely be run again. Do not commit `.env` or use development credentials outside local development.
 
 To run focused PostgreSQL constraint tests, set `TEST_DATABASE_URL` to a disposable database where the test user can create and drop schemas, then run `npm run test:db`. The tests create and remove an isolated schema.
 
 The authentication endpoints are `POST /auth/login` with `{ "email": "...", "password": "..." }` (returns a one-hour bearer token) and `GET /auth/me` with `Authorization: ****** (returns the authenticated user's local roles). Run `npm run test:auth` for password-hash and token validation tests.
 
 The backend currently includes authentication and local-role authorization middleware, but announcement routes, workers, account seeding, and the frontend are not yet implemented.

 # Part A: The design
 
 ## 1. Data model
 
 - **`locals`** stores each union local. **`users`** stores authentication identity only; it has no global member/leader role. **`local_members`** stores a user's local-specific member profile, including name, contact details, `classification_id`, and active/retired/suspended status. **`local_leaders`** grants leadership access for a specific local. Both local-access tables use `(local_id, user_id)` as a primary or unique key, with foreign keys to `locals` and `users`. A user can have different or multiple local relationships without those permissions becoming global.
 - **`classifications`** stores work classifications scoped to a local, with a unique `(local_id, id)` key. `local_members` references it using `(local_id, classification_id)`, preventing a profile from using another local's classification.
 - **`local_members`** has its own UUID `id`, a foreign key `user_id` to `users`, and unique `(local_id, user_id)` and `(local_id, id)` keys. Thus recipient `member_id` always means `local_members.id`, never the authentication `users.id`.
 - **`announcements`** belongs to a local and stores its author, title, body, push preview, acknowledgement requirement, draft/approval/send state, and relevant timestamps. Its author is constrained by a composite foreign key `(local_id, author_user_id)` to `local_leaders`; approval, when recorded, is likewise tied to a leader in that local. Give announcements a unique `(local_id, id)` key for downstream composite references.
 - **`announcement_recipients`** has UUID `id`, `local_id`, `announcement_id`, and `member_id`, with `(announcement_id, member_id)` unique and `(local_id, id)` unique. Composite foreign keys `(local_id, announcement_id)` and `(local_id, member_id)` reference the corresponding announcement and `local_members` keys. Materialize these rows from the eligible audience at send time: they are the audience snapshot, not a live query whose membership changes later. Keep push-provider state separate from `read_at`, `acknowledged_at`, and nullable RSVP (`coming` / `can't`); no RSVP is distinct from “can't.”
 - **`outbox_jobs`** has UUID `id`, `local_id`, `recipient_id` (the recipient row's `announcement_recipients.id`), status, attempt count, `available_at`, and lease fields such as `lease_until`. A unique `(local_id, recipient_id)` permits one durable job per recipient; a composite foreign key `(local_id, recipient_id)` references `announcement_recipients (local_id, id)`. Workers therefore process the stored local and recipient row, not a client-supplied audience.
 - **`send_requests`** records the send idempotency key, local, leader user, announcement, and request hash. A unique `(local_id, leader_user_id, idempotency_key)` scopes key reuse; matching retries return the recorded send, while a different request hash is rejected. Its leader reference is constrained to `(local_id, leader_user_id)` in `local_leaders`.
 - **`delivery_attempts`** records each push attempt against its recipient, including attempt time and provider outcome, so retries do not erase history. Use a foreign key to `announcement_recipients`; use a stable provider idempotency key per recipient if the provider supports one.
 
 Use PostgreSQL `CHECK` constraints or enums for finite status/action values and checks for valid approval state/timestamp combinations. Index audience selection on `local_members (local_id, status, classification_id)`, announcement listings on `(local_id, created_at)`, recipient counts/lookups on `(local_id, announcement_id, push_status)` and `(announcement_id, read_at)` / `(announcement_id, acknowledged_at)`, outbox claiming on `(status, available_at)` and lease recovery on `(status, lease_until)`, and attempt history on `(recipient_id, attempted_at)`. Primary keys and unique constraints provide indexes for their keys; add indexes on other foreign-key columns used for joins and lookups.
 
 These constraints reject invalid cross-local references and duplicate recipient records; they do not replace endpoint authorization checks. Likewise, a unique recipient row does not guarantee exactly-once delivery by an external push provider.
 
 ## 2. The send path
 
 The authenticated Express endpoint verifies the leader's local permission and that the announcement is approved. The client supplies an idempotency key for the send operation. In one PostgreSQL transaction, the endpoint records the key and request hash in `send_requests`, snapshots eligible members into `announcement_recipients`, creates **one `outbox_jobs` row per recipient**, and marks the announcement as sending. A unique constraint on the scoped key makes a matching repeated request return the original send result rather than create a new audience; reusing the key with a different request hash is rejected. Recipient and outbox uniqueness also prevent duplicate rows/jobs.
 
 After commit, the endpoint returns an accepted/in-progress response; it does not wait for all pushes. Workers claim small batches of ready outbox rows in short transactions using row locks such as `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, recording a lease and attempt count. Each job supplies its stored `local_id` and `recipient_id`; workers load and verify that recipient and its member profile in that local, then call the provider outside the transaction and persist the outcome. Transient errors are rescheduled with backoff; permanent errors or exhausted retries are marked failed for review. If a worker crashes, its lease expires and another worker can reclaim the job. A stable provider idempotency key per recipient and announcement prevents repeated provider sends when supported. Without provider support, a crash after provider acceptance but before recording success leaves an ambiguous result: retrying can duplicate a push, while not retrying can lose it. Exactly-once external push delivery cannot be guaranteed in that case.
 
 Push is only a prompt. Members fetch their persisted callouts through the authenticated API and can sync after reconnecting, so being offline or missing a push does not remove access. Provider outcomes remain separate from read, acknowledgment, and RSVP actions.
 
 ## 3. The two rules, by design
 
 **Rule 1—local isolation and roles:** Express authenticates requests and derives the user identity from a verified credential, never a client-supplied role. Default-deny authorization checks the user's membership or leadership relationship for the specific local and action on every endpoint; queries are scoped to that local. Composite foreign keys reject cross-local references. PostgreSQL row-level security can add defense in depth if the app role cannot bypass it and each transaction sets its local context safely. Workers use a separate least-privilege identity and validate job local/recipient references. Append audit records for sensitive reads and mutations, including actor, local, action, resource, outcome, and timestamp; exclude credentials and unnecessary personal data.
 
 **Rule 2—duplicate processing:** The transactional send snapshot, unique recipient/job constraints, persisted idempotency key, and leased outbox claims make request retries and worker restarts safe at the database/job level. Provider idempotency is needed to prevent duplicate external pushes across the acceptance/recording crash window; without provider support, exactly-once push delivery cannot be guaranteed.

Implemented the announcement draft and send API.

### Endpoints

- `POST /locals/:localId/announcements` — creates a leader-authored draft. Validates title, body, acknowledgement flag, and optional push preview.
- `POST /locals/:localId/announcements/:announcementId/send` — requires an `Idempotency-Key`; optionally accepts a local classification filter. The leader’s explicit Send action records approval and transactionally stores the request, active-member recipient snapshot, one outbox job per recipient, and announcement `sending` state. Returns `202 Accepted`.

Both routes authenticate the user and check leadership for the requested local in PostgreSQL. Cross-local announcement/classification access is rejected. Reusing an idempotency key with the same announcement and audience returns the original result; changing the request under that key returns `409 Conflict`. Empty audiences return `422`.

### Files changed

- Added [routes.ts](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/backend/src/announcements/routes.ts) and mounted the router in [app.ts](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/backend/src/app.ts).
- Added PostgreSQL integration coverage in [announcements.test.ts](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/backend/src/announcements/announcements.test.ts), with `test:announcements` in [package.json](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/backend/package.json).
- Updated [README.md](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/README.md) with endpoint/auth details and test instructions.

### Validation

The TypeScript build passed. PostgreSQL-backed announcement tests passed, including classification filtering, same-key replay and conflict, cross-local authorization, and concurrent sends (same key and distinct keys). Schema, seed, and auth tests also passed; production dependency audit reported zero vulnerabilities, and `git diff --check` passed.

Delivery workers, provider integration, AI, frontend, and the optional load-balancer bonus remain unimplemented.

 # Requirements
 
 ## Confirmed requirements
 - Build a callout/announcement feature for union locals. A leader sends to one local, optionally narrowed by work classification; members need to see callouts even if they are offline when sent.
 - Enforce local-level data isolation for both members and leadership, and prevent members from using leadership permissions. Union membership/contact data is sensitive.
 - Retries and worker restarts must not cause the same member to receive a callout twice. Track each recipient's outcome and actions, rather than only aggregate announcement counts.
 - Push is not a reliable measure of receipt: about 5–10% of pushes may silently fail, and members may be offline for hours or days. Leaders need timely visibility into who has read, acknowledged, or plans to attend.
 - AI-generated title, body, and push preview (120 characters or fewer) must remain a draft until a human leader approves sending.
 
 ## Assumptions
 - Unless confirmed otherwise, the send audience is active members of the selected local, optionally filtered by classification; retired and suspended members are excluded.
 - No response is required by default. Acknowledgment and an attendance RSVP ("coming" / "can't") are distinct actions; RSVP is needed for the design, but not the required build slice.
 - Members can retrieve a sent callout after reconnecting; push is a prompt, not the only way to access it. No delivery-time or availability SLA is specified.
 - "No duplicates" applies to both creating duplicate recipient records and sending duplicate notifications on retries. Whether this can be guaranteed at the push-provider boundary depends on provider behavior and needs to be defined.
 
 ## Concerns and gaps
 - The question about members outside a local seeing apprentices' contact information may indicate an existing exposure, not just a future requirement. Treat this as a potential incident to investigate and contain before relying on a new feature's access controls.
 - A unique recipient record alone does not establish that a member was notified, received the callout, read it, acknowledged it, or RSVP'd. Those states must not be conflated, especially when push can fail silently.

Implemented the member-facing announcement APIs.

### Endpoints

- `GET /locals/:localId/member/announcements` — lists sent announcements with recipient status for the authenticated member’s local membership.
- `GET /locals/:localId/member/announcements/:announcementId` — reads an announcement only if the member has its recipient row; records `read_at` on first read.
- `POST /locals/:localId/member/announcements/:announcementId/acknowledge` — acknowledges only a targeted, sent announcement that requires acknowledgement. Returns `409` if acknowledgement is not required and `404` for non-recipients or inaccessible announcements.

All routes check local membership in PostgreSQL, and their data queries also match the authenticated user to the recipient row. Reads and acknowledgements update existing recipient records; acknowledgements preserve their first timestamps, including concurrent or repeated requests.

 # CrewLink
 
 ## Backend setup
 
 The backend uses Express, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL 13 or later is required for `gen_random_uuid()`.
 
 1. Create a PostgreSQL database and user (or use an existing local development database).
 2. From the `backend` directory, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `DATABASE_URL` to the connection string for that database. `PORT` defaults to `4000`.
    Set `JWT_SECRET` to a unique cryptographically random secret of at least 32 bytes; the API will not start without it. Do not reuse the example value or commit the secret.
 3. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
 4. Apply the initial schema with `npm run db:migrate`.
 5. Seed the assessment data with `npm run db:seed`. It is safe to rerun.
 6. Start the development server with `npm run dev`. Check `http://localhost:4000/health` for database connectivity.
 7. Run `npm run build` to type-check and compile; run `npm start` to start the compiled server.
 
 The migration is tracked in `schema_migrations` and can safely be run again. Do not commit `.env` or use development credentials outside local development.
 
 To run focused PostgreSQL constraint tests, set `TEST_DATABASE_URL` to a disposable database where the test user can create and drop schemas, then run `npm run test:db`. The tests create and remove an isolated schema.

The leader's explicit Send action approves the draft. A successful send returns `202 Accepted`; recipient snapshots and outbox jobs are committed before that response, while provider delivery is not implemented yet.

 # CrewLink
 
 ## Backend setup
 
 The backend uses Express, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL 13 or later is required for `gen_random_uuid()`.
 
 1. Create a PostgreSQL database and user (or use an existing local development database).
 2. From the `backend` directory, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `DATABASE_URL` to the connection string for that database. `PORT` defaults to `4000`.
    Set `JWT_SECRET` to a unique cryptographically random secret of at least 32 bytes; the API will not start without it. Do not reuse the example value or commit the secret.
 3. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
 4. Apply the schema with `npm run db:migrate`.
 5. Seed the assessment data with `npm run db:seed`. It is safe to rerun.
 6. Start the development server with `npm run dev`. Check `http://localhost:4000/health` for database connectivity.

 # Requirements
 
 ## Confirmed requirements
 - Build a callout/announcement feature for union locals. A leader sends to one local, optionally narrowed by work classification; members need to see callouts even if they are offline when sent.
 - Enforce local-level data isolation for both members and leadership, and prevent members from using leadership permissions. Union membership/contact data is sensitive.
 - Retries and worker restarts must not cause the same member to receive a callout twice. Track each recipient's outcome and actions, rather than only aggregate announcement counts.
 - Push is not a reliable measure of receipt: about 5–10% of pushes may silently fail, and members may be offline for hours or days. Leaders need timely visibility into who has read, acknowledged, or plans to attend.
 - AI-generated title, body, and push preview (120 characters or fewer) must remain a draft until a human leader approves sending.
 
 ## Assumptions
 - Unless confirmed otherwise, the send audience is active members of the selected local, optionally filtered by classification; retired and suspended members are excluded.
 - No response is required by default. Acknowledgment and an attendance RSVP ("coming" / "can't") are distinct actions; RSVP is needed for the design, but not the required build slice.
 - Members can retrieve a sent callout after reconnecting; push is a prompt, not the only way to access it. No delivery-time or availability SLA is specified.
 - "No duplicates" applies to both creating duplicate recipient records and sending duplicate notifications on retries. Whether this can be guaranteed at the push-provider boundary depends on provider behavior and needs to be defined.
 
 ## Concerns and gaps
 - The question about members outside a local seeing apprentices' contact information may indicate an existing exposure, not just a future requirement. Treat this as a potential incident to investigate and contain before relying on a new feature's access controls.
 - A unique recipient record alone does not establish that a member was notified, received the callout, read it, acknowledged it, or RSVP'd. Those states must not be conflated, especially when push can fail silently.
 - "Immediately" and "before I leave the hall" have no measurable timing target; no RSVP deadline, edit policy, or rule for late audience changes is given.
 
 ## Open questions for Denise
 1. Who is eligible for a callout: active members only, and how should classification changes or membership changes after sending affect it? Assumed active members at send time.
 2. What does "immediately" mean, and which notification states should leadership see as sent or delivered when a push fails or a member is offline? Assumed send begins promptly, with recipient-level progress and later access.
 3. Should attendance responses be optional or required, by what deadline, and may members change them? Assumed optional unless a callout explicitly requests an RSVP.
 
 # Part A: The design
 
 ## 1. Data model
 
 - **`locals`** stores each union local. **`users`** stores authentication identity only; it has no global member/leader role. **`local_members`** stores a user's local-specific member profile, including name, contact details, `classification_id`, and active/retired/suspended status. **`local_leaders`** grants leadership access for a specific local. Both local-access tables use `(local_id, user_id)` as a primary or unique key, with foreign keys to `locals` and `users`. A user can have different or multiple local relationships without those permissions becoming global.
 - **`classifications`** stores work classifications scoped to a local, with a unique `(local_id, id)` key. `local_members` references it using `(local_id, classification_id)`, preventing a profile from using another local's classification.
 - **`local_members`** has its own UUID `id`, a foreign key `user_id` to `users`, and unique `(local_id, user_id)` and `(local_id, id)` keys. Thus recipient `member_id` always means `local_members.id`, never the authentication `users.id`.
 - **`announcements`** belongs to a local and stores its author, title, body, push preview, acknowledgement requirement, draft/approval/send state, and relevant timestamps. Its author is constrained by a composite foreign key `(local_id, author_user_id)` to `local_leaders`; approval, when recorded, is likewise tied to a leader in that local. Give announcements a unique `(local_id, id)` key for downstream composite references.
 - **`announcement_recipients`** has UUID `id`, `local_id`, `announcement_id`, and `member_id`, with `(announcement_id, member_id)` unique and `(local_id, id)` unique. Composite foreign keys `(local_id, announcement_id)` and `(local_id, member_id)` reference the corresponding announcement and `local_members` keys. Materialize these rows from the eligible audience at send time: they are the audience snapshot, not a live query whose membership changes later. Keep push-provider state separate from `read_at`, `acknowledged_at`, and nullable RSVP (`coming` / `can't`); no RSVP is distinct from “can't.”

 # CrewLink
 
 ## Backend setup
 
 The backend uses Express, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL 13 or later is required for `gen_random_uuid()`.
 
 1. Create a PostgreSQL database and user (or use an existing local development database).
 2. From the `backend` directory, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `DATABASE_URL` to the connection string for that database. `PORT` defaults to `4000`.
    Set `JWT_SECRET` to a unique cryptographically random secret of at least 32 bytes; the API will not start without it. To enable AI draft suggestions, set `AI_API_KEY` for an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions API; `AI_API_URL` and `AI_MODEL` default to the values in `.env.example`. Never commit API credentials. With no AI key configured, the AI drafting endpoint returns `503` while manual draft creation remains available.
 3. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
 4. Apply the schema with `npm run db:migrate`.
 5. Seed the assessment data with `npm run db:seed`. It is safe to rerun.
 6. Start the development server with `npm run dev`. Check `http://localhost:4000/health` for database connectivity.
 7. Run `npm run build` to type-check and compile; run `npm start` to start the compiled server.
 
 Migrations are tracked in `schema_migrations` and can safely be run again. Do not commit `.env` or use development credentials outside local development.
 
 To run focused PostgreSQL constraint tests, set `TEST_DATABASE_URL` to a disposable database where the test user can create and drop schemas, then run `npm run test:db`. The tests create and remove an isolated schema.
 
 The authentication endpoints are `POST /auth/login` with `{ "email": "...", "password": "..." }` (returns a one-hour bearer token) and `GET /auth/me` with `Authorization: ****** (returns the authenticated user's local roles). Local leaders can create drafts with `POST /locals/:localId/announcements` and send with `POST /locals/:localId/announcements/:announcementId/send`, using `Authorization: ****** Send requests require an `Idempotency-Key` header and accept an optional `{ "classificationId": "<uuid>" }` body. The leader's explicit Send action approves the draft. A successful send returns `202 Accepted`; recipient snapshots and outbox jobs are committed before that response, and delivery is handled asynchronously by the mock worker described below.
 
 Members can list their sent callouts with `GET /locals/:localId/member/announcements`, read a recipient callout with `GET /locals/:localId/member/announcements/:announcementId`, and acknowledge an acknowledgement-required callout with `POST /locals/:localId/member/announcements/:announcementId/acknowledge`. All require `Authorization: ******; list/read/acknowledgement queries additionally require a recipient row linked to that member's local membership. Reading and acknowledging save their first timestamps; repeated reads and acknowledgements preserve those timestamps.
 
 Run the mock push outbox worker in a separate terminal with `npm run worker` after migrations and seeding. Workers claim jobs using `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, lease them, recover expired leases, and retry transient failures with bounded exponential backoff. Each outcome is recorded in `delivery_attempts`; recipient push state becomes `delivered` only after a successful provider response, and permanent or exhausted failures become `failed`. The mock provider persists successful idempotency keys in PostgreSQL so a worker restart reuses the same delivery rather than creating a second mock delivery. A real external provider still needs to honor the persisted idempotency key to protect against duplicate external deliveries.

 # CrewLink
 
 ## Backend setup
 
 The backend uses Express, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL 13 or later is required for `gen_random_uuid()`.
 
 1. Create a PostgreSQL database and user (or use an existing local development database).
 2. From the `backend` directory, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `DATABASE_URL` to the connection string for that database. `PORT` defaults to `4000`.
    Set `JWT_SECRET` to a unique cryptographically random secret of at least 32 bytes; the API will not start without it. To enable AI draft suggestions, set `AI_API_KEY` for an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions API; `AI_API_URL` and `AI_MODEL` default to the values in `.env.example`. Never commit API credentials. With no AI key configured, the AI drafting endpoint returns `503` while manual draft creation remains available.
 3. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
 4. Apply the schema with `npm run db:migrate`.
 5. Seed the assessment data with `npm run db:seed`. It is safe to rerun.
 6. Start the development server with `npm run dev`. Check `http://localhost:4000/health` for database connectivity.
 7. Run `npm run build` to type-check and compile; run `npm start` to start the compiled server.
 
 Migrations are tracked in `schema_migrations` and can safely be run again. Do not commit `.env` or use development credentials outside local development.
 
 To run focused PostgreSQL constraint tests, set `TEST_DATABASE_URL` to a disposable database where the test user can create and drop schemas, then run `npm run test:db`. The tests create and remove an isolated schema.
 
 The authentication endpoints are `POST /auth/login` with `{ "email": "...", "password": "..." }` (returns a one-hour bearer token) and `GET /auth/me` with `Authorization: ****** (returns the authenticated user's local roles). Local leaders can create drafts with `POST /locals/:localId/announcements` and send with `POST /locals/:localId/announcements/:announcementId/send`, using `Authorization: ****** Send requests require an `Idempotency-Key` header and accept an optional `{ "classificationId": "<uuid>" }` body. The leader's explicit Send action approves the draft. A successful send returns `202 Accepted`; recipient snapshots and outbox jobs are committed before that response, and delivery is handled asynchronously by the mock worker described below.
 
 Members can list their sent callouts with `GET /locals/:localId/member/announcements`, read a recipient callout with `GET /locals/:localId/member/announcements/:announcementId`, and acknowledge an acknowledgement-required callout with `POST /locals/:localId/member/announcements/:announcementId/acknowledge`. All require `Authorization: ******; list/read/acknowledgement queries additionally require a recipient row linked to that member's local membership. Reading and acknowledging save their first timestamps; repeated reads and acknowledgements preserve those timestamps.
 
 Run the mock push outbox worker in a separate terminal with `npm run worker` after migrations and seeding. Workers claim jobs using `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, lease them, recover expired leases, and retry transient failures with bounded exponential backoff. Each outcome is recorded in `delivery_attempts`; recipient push state becomes `delivered` only after a successful provider response, and permanent or exhausted failures become `failed`. The mock provider persists successful idempotency keys in PostgreSQL so a worker restart reuses the same delivery rather than creating a second mock delivery. A real external provider still needs to honor the persisted idempotency key to protect against duplicate external deliveries.
 
 Local leaders can request a suggested callout draft with `POST /locals/:localId/announcements/ai-draft` and a JSON body such as `{ "notes": "messy meeting notes..." }`. It returns a saved `draft` announcement with a suggested title, body, and push preview (at most 120 characters). The AI only drafts text: it does not select recipients, approve, or send. Review and edit the stored draft, then use the existing send endpoint to explicitly approve and start delivery. Missing AI credentials return `503`; provider failures or invalid model output return `502` without creating an announcement.
 
 Run `npm run test:seed` against a disposable PostgreSQL database to verify repeated seeding does not duplicate data. Run `npm run test:announcements`, `npm run test:ai`, `npm run test:members`, and `npm run test:worker` with `TEST_DATABASE_URL` set to a disposable PostgreSQL database to test the APIs and worker behavior. The frontend is not yet implemented.
 
 ## TEST ACCOUNTS
 
 These credentials are for local assessment only. The seed contains synthetic accounts; never reuse these passwords or seed credentials in production.

response.value:
## Audit results

The frontend/API workflow is integrated: leaders sign in, see only locals returned by `/auth/me`, select a classification, create or load drafts, generate editable AI suggestions, and explicitly send. Each local-scoped API route independently checks leadership authorization; the client’s local selection is not treated as authorization. The dashboard shows recipient, delivered, read, and acknowledged counts, refreshed every four seconds.

Member list/read/acknowledgement routes remain recipient- and local-scoped. AI output is validated and saved as an unapproved draft. Sending snapshots recipients and creates outbox jobs transactionally; retries and worker recovery retain per-recipient tracking.

The README has the exact `## TEST ACCOUNTS` heading. Its fenced JSON parses and includes all four seeded logins, the expected seeded announcement and cross-local member IDs, and 13 documented endpoints with auth details.

## Verified fixes

- The seeded announcement had recipient records but no outbox jobs, despite the README saying those jobs were ready. Seeding now creates one job per recipient idempotently; the seed test verifies **2,000 jobs** after repeat seeding.
- A permanently failed delivery could leave its parent announcement marked `sent`. The worker now marks the announcement `failed` when any recipient job fails; a focused worker test verifies this outcome.

## Validation

- Backend TypeScript build and Next.js production build passed.
- All PostgreSQL-backed schema, auth, seed, leader API, AI, member API, and worker test suites passed.
- Migrations applied twice successfully; seed ran twice with counts of **2 locals, 2,200 members, 2,000 recipients, 2,000 outbox jobs, and 1 sent announcement**.
- `git diff --check` passed; frontend dependency audit found **zero vulnerabilities**.

Changed files include [frontend/](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/frontend), [README.md](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/README.md), [routes.ts](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/backend/src/announcements/routes.ts), [app.ts](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/backend/src/app.ts), [seed.ts](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/backend/src/db/seed.ts), and [outboxWorker.ts](C:/Users/Alkesh/Desktop/avialdo/Availdo-solutions/crewLink-Challenge/backend/src/workers/outboxWorker.ts), plus related tests, environment configuration, and `.gitignore`.
